https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: A Lebanese boy removes his damaged bicycle from his destroyed home in south Lebanon on Wednesday after an Israeli airstrike. Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/AP View image in fullscreen A Lebanese boy removes his damaged bicycle from his destroyed home in south Lebanon on Wednesday after an Israeli airstrike. Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Israel Israel strikes southern Lebanon killing one and injuring 11 Hits on two towns among deadliest bombings since start of June ceasefire William Christou in Beirut Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.34 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Israeli airstrike in south Lebanon killed one person and injured 11, the Lebanese ministry of health said, in one of Israel’s deadliest bombings since the start of the June ceasefire. Israel carried out an airstrike in the town of Tebnine, south Lebanon hitting a cemetery, the Lebanese health ministry said. It said the town of al-Mansouri, also in south Lebanon, was bombed too, forcing families to flee. The Israeli military issued a displacement order about 30 minutes before the strike, saying it was destroying Hezbollah’s infrastructure in the area in response to the group’s “violation of the ceasefire”. Two Israeli troops were killed and seven wounded in an explosion in south Lebanon on Wednesday, with the origin unknown. In recent weeks, Israeli troops have been wounded by booby-trapped vehicles and mines laid by Hezbollah in south Lebanon. View image in fullscreen Israeli tanks in south Lebanon on Wednesday. Photograph: EPA Wednesday was the first time Israel has issued a displacement order since the start of the June ceasefire. Such orders were a near daily occurrence during the most recent round of Hezbollah-Israel fighting, which started on 2 March and displaced more than 1 million people in Lebanon. Since the June ceasefire, Israel has occupied swathes of Lebanon as part of a so-called security zone. It has continued bombing parts of the area and killing people who have come near. It is a similar approach to in Gaza, where Israel occupies more than 60% of the strip under what it calls its “yellow line”, and continues to carry out bombings there. Earlier this year, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he had ordered the army to seize control of 70% of the Gaza strip . Gaza 'yellow zone' More than 1,200 people have been killed in Gaza since the beginning of the October ceasefire. At least 26 Palestinians were killed by Israeli strikes in the strip over the past weekend. In Lebanon, Israel has continued mass demolitions in areas it occupies, including a blast last week that used 700 tons of explosives around Beaufort Castle, outside Nabatieh. Israel has said it is targeting Hezbollah infrastructure, but rights groups, including Human Rights Watch, say the indiscriminate nature of the explosives could comprise the war crime of wanton destruction. Talks between the Lebanese government and Israel for a more permanent peace are continuing, with the two sides meeting in Rome on Tuesday. The Lebanese government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal, while Israel wants the disarmament of Hezbollah. View image in fullscreen A woman and child stand next to Lebanese military vehicles in Zawtar al Gharbiya, southern Lebanon, one of the pilot zones. Photograph: EPA The meetings in Rome are the seventh between the two sides, with talks expected to focus on the Ali Taher area in south Lebanon, where Israeli troops have been conducting detonations. So far, negotiations have resulted three “pilot zones” in south Lebanon where the Lebanese army has assumed control. The two sides are using these as tests of whether the Lebanese army can prevent Hezbollah from entering and can continue to dismantle the group’s infrastructure there. Progress in the pilot zones is slow and the Lebanese government has asked for a quicker Israeli withdrawal, which Israel is unlikely to agree to. The fighting this year started after Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel on 2 March in retaliation for the killing of Iran’s late supreme leader, Ali Khamenei. Israel then began a bombing campaign and invaded south Lebanon. Israel has since killed 4,321 people in Lebanon, while at least 40 Israelis, 38 of them troops, were killed by Hezbollah. https://www.newsday.com/news/nation/tate.text: Andrew Tate, left, watches his brother Tristan speak, outside a police station in Voluntari, Romania, May 21, 2025. Credit: AP/Vadim Ghirda By The Associated Press August 10, 2026 10:41 pm Share MIAMI — Prosecutors want social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate to remain in federal custody, arguing Monday that the brothers are a flight risk and a danger to the community, as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking. Three days after defense attorneys filed a motion for release, prosecutors filed their response in Miami federal court, where a hearing on Thursday will determine if the brothers should stay in jail or be released during what could be a monthslong extradition process. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. The detention hearing is likely to be the first time the Tates leave the Federal Detention Center in Miami since making a brief court appearance two days after their July 18 arrest. The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in the Tates' long-running international legal saga spanning the U.S., Britain and Romania. Prosecutors claim a ‘heightened risk of flight’ According to the U.S. Attorney's Office filing, the Tates should be detained pending their extradition hearing because they cannot overcome the strong presumption against bail in international extradition cases. Sign up for the Breaking News newsletter Get the latest breaking news as it happens. By clicking Sign up, you agree to our privacy policy . The serious pending U.K. charges involving human trafficking and violent rapes and assaults against multiple victims, along with allegations in Romania that the Tates attempted to intimidate witnesses, present a clear public safety concern, prosecutors say. “That the Tates also claim to maintain multiple passports and identities, have access to excessive wealth and influence in numerous countries, and are stridently unwilling to voluntarily return to face prosecution in the United Kingdom, collectively demonstrate a heightened risk of flight that no amount of bond could overcome,” the filing says. Andrew Tate, right, and his brother Tristan arrive at an event, April 11, 2026, in Miami. Credit: AP/Julia Demaree Nikhinson The defense motion filed Friday acknowledges there is a presumption against bond in extradition proceedings but argues that release can be granted in special circumstances. It says the Tates’ high profile makes it nearly impossible for them to flee, and that they regularly post updates about their locations on social media. While prosecutors call the brothers a flight risk, their attorneys said they have proved they are not by complying with all pretrial restrictions in Romania, where they are accused of luring women for sexual exploitation. The U.K. has until mid-September to provide evidence to the State Department to support extradition, meaning the brothers could spend months in FDC Miami before the proceedings are resolved, the defense motion says. No date has been set for an extradition hearing. They are being held in a special unit for their own protection. Legal troubles follow the Tate brothers The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. The former professional kickboxers, who have dual U.S. and U.K. citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn't expect any help from the president. British prosecutors said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in southeastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case hasn't moved forward due to legal and procedural problems. The Tates' attorneys have said the Romanian court has granted a U.K. request for extradition that will take effect after Romanian proceedings conclude. Andrew Tate, 39, became famous a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was ejected from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman. He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. Tristan Tate, 38, has worked with his brother on multiple businesses, including the production of online webcam pornography. Streaming Now FBI, police seize 23 illegal guns, drugs from home ... https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Nuwakot in Nepal. The UN’s scientific advisory body warned in 2023 that ice-bound landmasses would become more unstable. Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Nuwakot in Nepal. The UN’s scientific advisory body warned in 2023 that ice-bound landmasses would become more unstable. Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Climate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warn Unusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastrophe Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates What caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet? Jonathan Watts Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.25 EDT First published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 14.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The devastating flash flood that has ripped through the border communities of Nepal and Tibet has heightened fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions, threatening millions of people. Satellite imagery suggests a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the deadly torrent of mud, water and ice that tore along the Bhotekoshi River on Wednesday. It swept away buildings and roads and left at least 360 dead and 1,400 missing. A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was initially blamed for the collapse. However, it is now thought to have been caused by the huge wall of ice that crashed down on to the north slope of Langtang Lirung, a 7,000-metre (23,000ft) mountain, the impact of which registered a magnitude of 5.2. “Additional analysis of long-period seismic waves indicates that the seismic energy was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow,” the US Geological Survey said . A map showing the area where the flash flood hit. The ice-rock avalanche pushed boulders and other debris into the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River. Water levels in rivers downstream rose by between 7 and 9 metres within 30 minutes, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, an intergovernmental scientific institution. Scientists are still examining the precise mechanics of the Himalayan disaster, but many observe that glaciers and permafrost around the world are being weakened by global heating, caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal. View image in fullscreen Flooding in the Bhotekoshi River has affected low-lying areas along the riverbanks and nearby homes in Nuwakot, Nepal. Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock The detachment of a chunk of the glacier wall came amid unusual heat that was likely to have melted the ice that bound the splintered bedrock together. Two days before the collapse, the ground temperature hit its highest point in the last two years, according to Dr Hamish Pritchard, a glaciologist with the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors 6 miles (10km) away from the site. “These high temperatures would have weakened the snowpack, filled crevasses with water and thawed the bonds between ice and rock that hold these glaciers in place,” he told the Science Media Centre. A series of intense heatwaves has hit the region since early this year and affected countries around the world. Another factor here was the monsoon season, which saturated the soil and swelled rivers. A map showing the timeline of the disaster. Disasters like this were foretold. In 2023 the UN’s top scientific advisory body warned that previously ice-bound landmasses – from permafrost tundra to mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose. “Every increment of warming will multiply and intensify future hazards from cryosphere regions,” observed the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in its sixth synthesis report. “Floods, landslides and freshwater shortages from glacier retreat and snow loss pose a serious threat to mountain regions across the world.” Average global temperatures are nudging closer to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Even faster warming is occurring in alpine and polar regions because the loss of snow and ice is removing the thermal insulation of the land. Dr Richard Waller, a senior lecturer in physical geography at Keele University, said: “The progressive loss of snow and glacier ice results in the surface being less reflective, so it absorbs more solar energy and heats up. In combination with atmospheric warming, this is leading to the melting of mountain permafrost. “Think of the high mountains like this as shattered bedrock glued together by ice-filled joints. As the permafrost and the ice-filled joints melt, then there’s the potential for these types of catastrophic failure.” View image in fullscreen A destroyed building in Devighat, Nuwakot. Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/AP The thaw is altering the shape, colour and solidity of the landscape, creating or expanding glacial meltwater lakes and, in the long term, threatening the origin of many rivers and the drinking supplies of populations downstream. In many parts of Asia, hundreds of millions of people depend on the rivers such as the Ganges and the Brahmaputra that descend from the glaciers. Scientists have high confidence that glacier retreat is caused by human-driven global heating. This has caused glacier collapses from the Alps to the Andes. In the Langtang catchment area in Nepal, glacier loss rates have increased more than fourfold since 1964, a study has shown . TImeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainer This has contributed to a loss of life on multiple occasions. A smaller flood hit the Bhotekoshi River in July 2025 and in 2015, the Langtang Lirung mountain was hit by an earthquake-induced avalanche that destroyed Langtang village. As emergency services look for bodies and humanitarian relief groups mobilise for survivors, others are asking where next. Waller said any high mountain areas with glaciers and permafrost could be vulnerable, including the European Alps, Caucasus, Himalayas, Andes and beyond. As glacier weakening accelerates, Pritchard called for greater disaster preparedness. “More avalanches and more floods are inevitable, particularly as lakes grow in front of the retreating glaciers,” he said. “Early warning systems are urgently needed to protect the people living in these valleys.” Explore more on these topics Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Nepal Tibet China South and central Asia Climate crisis news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Timeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainer Australian officials ‘working around the clock’ to check welfare of tourists missing in Nepal Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burst Search is on for at least 33 Britons missing after flash floods in Nepal and Tibet The Guardian view on the Nepal-Tibet floods: prepare for more climate-linked disasters Live Nepal flash flood: death toll nears 400 amid warning of fresh danger from rising lake water – latest updates ‘Tsunami from the sky:’ floods leave trail of devastation in Nepal and Tibet - The Latest How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.cei.int/ansa/178925.text: NATO jets shoot down drone in Latvian airspace: ministry (ANSA-AFP) - RIGA, AUG 14 - NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace, the country's defence ministry confirmed Friday, followed by an announcement from the military. The interception came against a backdrop of heightened concern in Europe over unauthorised drone activity, as the Russia-Ukraine war grinds on more than four years. NATO "fighter jets have successfully shot down a foreign unmanned aerial vehicle that had entered Latvia as a result of Russian electromagnetic warfare," the ministry wrote on X. The threat had ended, the armed forces said in a post on X, adding that allied fighter jets successfully destroyed the unmanned aerial vehicle that entered the NATO member state's airspace. The EU and NATO member state of about 1.9 million inhabitants shares a border with Russia to the east. It and other countries along the alliance's Eastern flank have experienced numerous drone incursions into its territory. (ANSA-AFP). Know-how Exchange Programme Call for Proposals 2026 now open! https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgqd.text: Image source, TCB Image caption, Hafidh Ameir Hassan kept a low profile and was rarely seen in public with the president By Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa Â and Â Hafsa Khalil Published 7 September 2026, 11:08 BST Updated 39 minutes ago The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has died while receiving treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar. Vice-president Deogratius Ndejembi - who made the official announcement of Ameir's death - said he had been suffering from a heart condition. He was buried at his family's residence in Kizimkazi, a village on the country's semi-autonomous island of Zanzibar, on Monday evening. Ameir was an agricultural academic who largely kept a low public profile. He became Tanzania's first First Gentleman after President Samia took office in 2021. In his announcement, Ndejembi said Ameir died at 08:00 local time (06:00 GMT) on Monday at the Emilio Mzena Memorial Hospital. The vice-president led tributes as he conveyed his condolences to Samia, as well as Ameir's family and friends. Kenyan President William Ruto said he received the news of his passing with "deep sorrow". "President Samia has lost a lifelong companion, her children a beloved father, and Tanzania a distinguished son," he wrote on social media. Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema also shared his condolences, saying that they "stand side by side" with the first family, and all of Tanzania during "this difficult time". Similarly, Burundi's President Ãvariste Ndayishimiye paid his respects and prayed for Samia and her family to have "comfort and strength in this difficult moment". "May he [God] grant eternal rest to the soul of Hafidh Ameir Hassan," he added. The First Gentleman rarely appeared in public alongside the president. He was only occasionally seen with her at official events. He married Samia in 1978, before she entered national politics. The couple had four children - three sons and a daughter - together. Their daughter, Wanu Hafidh Ameir, is also a politician who currently serves in Zanzibar's House of Representatives in the National Assembly. https://baltic-review.com/latvia-vocatio.text: Share Tweet 0 Vocational schools across Latvia are accepting additional applications through 30 September. A second chance after the school year begins Latvia’s vocational-education system is keeping an additional admissions window open for students who have not yet chosen their next step. On 19 September, Latvian Public Media reported that places were still available in a number of technical schools and vocational secondary schools, with applications continuing until 30 September. The development offers a practical alternative for young people who started the academic year elsewhere, changed their plans or have not enrolled at all. The State Education Development Agency, known by its Latvian acronym VIAA, says additional recruitment is taking place in institutions both in Riga and in the regions. The offer is aimed mainly at students finishing either ninth or twelfth grade, but the available routes differ depending on the programme. After ninth grade, students can enter four-year courses that combine a professional qualification with secondary education. Some programmes accepting students after twelfth grade can be completed in one to one and a half years. For families, the message is significant because the traditional September deadline does not necessarily close the door to further study. The remaining places are limited and can change quickly, so applicants are being encouraged to contact schools directly rather than rely only on general listings. ([lsm.lv](https://www.lsm.lv/raksts/zinas/latvija/19.09.2026-vel-var-pagut-iestaties-kada-no-tehnikumiem.a663883/?utm_source=openai)) Skills linked to everyday economic life The list of possible subjects reflects a broad interpretation of vocational education. VIAA names cook, assistant cook, electrical technician, welder, finishing-work technician, crop-production technician, heavy-vehicle mechanic, programming technician, make-up artist, clothing and styling specialist, road-construction machinery operator, car mechanic and mechatronics technician among the available options. In some schools, the vacancies also point to changing patterns of local demand. Jēkabpils Technology Technical School told Latvian Public Media that places remained available in areas including programming, cybersecurity, accounting and other subjects. At Jelgava Technical School, applicants could still enquire about surveying technology, furniture making, computer systems and programming. Riga Tourism and Creative Industries Technical School listed commercial work, restaurant cooking and hospitality services among its remaining options. The situation is not uniform. Some popular courses filled quickly, while others struggled to form a full group, particularly in smaller towns. The Jēkabpils school said that construction and landscape-technology groups in its Barkava branch had not attracted enough students to open in the first year, despite employers’ need for related skills. That contrast underlines the challenge facing vocational education: demand from the economy does not always translate into immediate demand from school-leavers. More students, but not every place filled Education Ministry data cited by Latvian Public Media indicate that the number of students in Latvia’s technical schools and vocational secondary schools has increased by almost 4% since 2020. The longer-term direction is therefore positive, even though institutions have not filled all of their planned places for the 2026/2027 academic year. The additional admissions round also reflects the fluidity of September. School representatives told Latvian Public Media that some young people change programmes after discovering that their first choice is not suitable, while others move from vocational education to general secondary school or make the opposite decision. That movement is part of the adjustment period rather than necessarily a sign of failure. Schools are preparing support for those joining after lessons have begun. Riga Tourism and Creative Industries Technical School said it has an internal system to help late entrants adapt and catch up with missed material. Jēkabpils Technology Technical School also said that additional consultations would be available. The support matters because a delayed start can otherwise become a barrier even when a student has found a suitable course. Support for students from outside the main cities According to VIAA, students admitted to state-funded places may receive a monthly scholarship of up to €150, depending on academic performance and other criteria. Schools can also offer dormitory accommodation when students travel from another town or municipality. Those provisions make the remaining places more accessible to families who would otherwise face the additional cost of relocation or daily travel. The participating institutions extend well beyond the capital. The current list includes schools in Jēkabpils, Jelgava, Kandava, Daugavpils and Višķi, Liepāja, Ogre, Rēzekne, Smiltene, Ventspils, Priekuļi, Cēsis and other locations. That geographic spread gives the admissions round a national character, while also showing how vocational education can connect regional communities with technical, service and agricultural skills. Applicants and parents should check each school’s current vacancies and admission requirements directly. Some programmes accept applications until 30 September, while others continue until places are filled. The immediate opportunity is practical rather than symbolic: students who are still undecided have several more days to enter a structured course, gain a recognised qualification and begin the school year with a route that can lead onward to employment or further study. https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuania_st.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuania sticks to 2030 Rail Baltica deadline despite Baltic agreement to extend it 2026-09-28 LETA/BNS/TBT Staff Photo: Tom from Pixabay VILNIUS - Lithuania is sticking to its original 2030 deadline for the first phase of the Rail Baltica project despite a Baltic agreement to extend the deadline to 2034, the country's transport minister said, according to business news portal Verslo Zinios. Transport Minister Juras Taminskas said Lithuania aims to complete the section from Kaunas to Panevezys by 2030, citing the project's critical importance for connectivity, security, military mobility and economic competitiveness. Mindaugas Ivanavicius, head of Rail Baltica in Lithuania, told the portal that LTG Infra, the infrastructure arm of the Lithuanian Railways group responsible for the project, is maintaining its pace, with design, procurement and construction work under way. The statement follows remarks by Latvian official Andris Kulbergas last week, who said the 2030 deadline was unrealistic, leading all three Baltic states to agree to postpone the first phase until 2034. This marked the first official acknowledgement by the Baltic states that the 2030 target was no longer feasible. The first phase, connecting the Baltic states to Europe with a single track, is estimated to cost 15.3 billion euros. The total cost, including the installation of a second track, could reach 23.8 billion euros. Rail Baltica will link Tallinn, Parnu, Riga, Panevezys, Kaunas, Vilnius and Warsaw.
